stops.name: San Juan, the house on the calle del Norte
stops.campa: A low adobe house of one room and a fig tree, raised by his mother Paula Albarracín with wool she wove herself on a loom set under the branches. Doña Paula's husband, José Clemente Sarmiento, is a militia captain of small means and large enthusiasms; the boy is their fifth child and their first son to live. He is named Faustino Valentín, and will call himself Domingo Faustino. He learns to read at four. In this house the poverty is total and the ambition is unembarrassed, and the two never afterward separate in him.

stops.name: San Juan, the Escuela de la Patria
stops.campa: The new republic, five years old and at war, opens schools before it opens roads. In San Juan the Escuela de la Patria is run by two Buenos Aires teachers, the brothers Ignacio and José Rodríguez, on the mutual method, with a discipline of medals and disgraces. The boy attends every day for six years and is never once absent, never once punished, and is made First Citizen of the class. He will remember the room exactly for the rest of his life, and will spend that life trying to reproduce it, multiplied, across a continent.

stops.name: San Juan, the six scholarships not drawn
stops.campa: Buenos Aires offers six places at the Colegio de Ciencias Morales to be filled by lot among the provinces. San Juan draws its names; his is not among them. There is no appeal and no second list, and the province has nothing else to give a poor boy with a memory like his. He is ten. The wound never closes: everything he afterward builds, the normal schools, the national colleges in every province, the eight hundred schoolhouses of his presidency, is a machine designed so that the lottery need never be run again.

stops.name: San Francisco del Monte de Oro, the first school
stops.campa: His uncle, the friar José de Oro, is exiled to a hamlet in the hills of San Luis, and the nephew goes with him. In a mud-walled room the two open a school: the friar teaching theology and politics to the boy, the boy, at fifteen, teaching letters to seven pupils, some of them older than himself. It is his first classroom and his first command. He rings the bell, he sets the copybooks, he keeps order. The teacher of a nation is made here, in a place with no road to it, out of a priest's disgrace.

stops.name: San Luis, the prisoner who taught his jailers
stops.campa: The unitarian cause collapses in Cuyo after the Rodeo de Chacón, and the young officer is taken and held on an estancia outside San Luis, at the mercy of a federal family that could have him shot on a whim. He does what he will always do with a locked room: he turns it into a school, teaching the household's sons their letters until the mother of the house protects him. Released, he crosses the cordillera into Chile on foot and horseback with nothing. It is the first of two exiles and the pattern of both.

stops.name: Pocuro, the schoolmaster at thirteen pesos a month
stops.campa: On the Chilean side of the Andes, in the valley of Aconcagua, a village called Pocuro hires the destitute Argentine to keep its school for thirteen pesos a month. He is twenty. He teaches by day and reads by night whatever crosses the pass: Franklin's autobiography above all, which he will say made him wish to be Franklin. The exile's first employment on foreign ground is the trade he was born to and will never truly leave, whatever else he becomes: minister, general, ambassador, president. He is a schoolmaster who at intervals ran a country.

stops.name: Valparaíso, the shop clerk and the English lessons
stops.campa: In the port he takes work as a shop assistant at half a wage, and spends a peso and a half of it on English lessons from an Englishman, plus the candle he burns reading past midnight. In six weeks he can read Scott; in a year and a half he has read sixty English volumes. He never learns to speak the language decently and never needs to. Valparaíso is where the provincial autodidact discovers that the world can be got at through print, and decides, permanently, that print is a public utility.

stops.name: Copiapó, foreman at the mine of La Colorada
stops.campa: North, into the copper and silver desert of Atacama, where he serves nearly three years as mayordomo of the mine called La Colorada: keeping accounts, driving barreteros, learning by hand the geology and metallurgy he will one day legislate into schools of mines at San Juan and Catamarca. He reads in the galleries. He is a working manager of a real enterprise, which few of his lettered contemporaries ever were, and it marks his politics forever: he will always be more interested in a smelter than in a sonnet.

stops.name: San Juan, El Zonda and the Colegio de Santa Rosa
stops.campa: Home at last, he founds two things in one year: a school for girls, the Colegio de Pensionistas de Santa Rosa de América, and a newspaper, El Zonda, printed on a press so poor that the whole paper is a single sheet. The school teaches young women in a province that has never educated any; the paper needles the federal governor until a punitive stamp tax kills it at six numbers. He has discovered his two permanent instruments, the classroom and the press, and that the second is the more dangerous.

stops.name: San Juan, the arrest and the beating
stops.campa: The federal reaction reaches Cuyo. He is seized in the street by the mazorca of Benavídez, struck about the head and face, and thrown into the cells; his mother and sisters petition, and he is released only on condition that he leave the country. He will carry the marks. His hatred of Rosas is not, from this night forward, a doctrine held at a distance but a personal quarrel between a beaten provincial schoolmaster and the man he holds responsible for every ignorance in the republic.

stops.name: Baños del Zonda, the charcoal on the wall
stops.campa: Riding out to the pass, the exile stops at the bathhouse in the Zonda gorge and writes on the wall in charcoal, beneath the arms of the republic, a sentence in French so that his pursuers will not read it: On ne tue point les idées. The government sends a commission to decipher the hieroglyph. Five years later the same words stand as the epigraph of Facundo, with his own Spanish rendering beside them: to men one cuts the throat; to ideas, not. He is wrong about the attribution, which he gives to Fortoul; he is not wrong about the proposition, and the ground has heard it first.
stops.quote: On ne tue point les idées.
stops.quote_source: Escrito con carbón en los Baños del Zonda, noviembre de 1840; llevado luego como epígrafe de Facundo (1845)

stops.name: Valparaíso, the pen taken up at El Mercurio
stops.campa: An unknown foreigner walks into the offices of El Mercurio with an article on the anniversary of Chacabuco and walks out a journalist. Within months he is the most read and most detested pen in Chile: a man with no degree, no family, no country and no manners, writing about everything. He will edit or found El Progreso, El Heraldo Nacional, La Crónica. The Chilean decade makes him: it gives an exiled provincial the one thing San Juan could not, a public, and it teaches him that a newspaper is a portable republic.
